Name order and compound surnames

Source: vignettes/name-order.Rmd
name-order.Rmd

Records list names in different orders: JOHN A SMITH, SMITH JOHN A, SMITH, JOHN. Nothing in the string says which order was used, so peopleparser guesses from how often each token is used as a given name or as a surname. This article explains that evidence, the rules that use it for names of two, three and more tokens, and the rules that keep compound surnames (VON KAMECKE, GARCIA LOPEZ) together.

The rules run after cleaning, on the tokens that are left once titles, credentials and suffixes are gone (see vignette("name-cleaning")).

The examples parse a few names with parse_names() and show the name columns as a table:

library(peopleparser)

show <- function(x, cols = c("first_name", "middle_name", "last_name")) {
  parse_names(x)[c("name", cols)] |> knitr::kable()
}

The evidence: first-name and surname counts

census.names counts how often each name is a first name and how often a surname in U.S. Census Bureau name files (see vignette("gender-scoring") for where the table comes from). get_census_data() looks up each token:

get_census_data(c("JOHN", "SMITH", "JORDAN", "TAYLOR", "LESLIE", "TSHEPO")) |> knitr::kable()
name ordinal male_value female_value first_name_value last_name_value
JOHN 1 3118620 6503 3125123 37363
SMITH 2 4102 897 4999 2369644
JORDAN 3 329734 122596 452330 200984
TAYLOR 4 95501 293715 389216 723758
LESLIE 5 52838 237654 290492 24015
TSHEPO 6 0 0 0 0

Some tokens are clearly one or the other (JOHN, SMITH), although in the 2020 lists even SMITH is a rare given name. Others are both: JORDAN and TAYLOR are common in both positions, and LESLIE is a common surname too. TSHEPO is in neither list.

check_if_surname() turns the counts into a yes/no: a token reads as a surname when more than half of its count is in the surname position. A token found in neither list reads as a surname.

x <- c("JOHN", "SMITH", "JORDAN", "TAYLOR", "LESLIE", "TSHEPO")
setNames(check_if_surname(x), x)
#>   JOHN  SMITH JORDAN TAYLOR LESLIE TSHEPO 
#>  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE   TRUE

determine_surname() picks the single most likely surname in a name. It uses each token’s surname share,

plast=1+nlast1+nfirst+nlast p_{last} = \frac{1 + n_{last}}{1 + n_{first} + n_{last}}

and ranks tokens in three tiers:

  1. known names that are overwhelmingly surnames (plast≥0.95p_{last} \ge 0.95), the more common first;
  2. tokens in neither list;
  3. all other names, by plastp_{last}.

Remaining ties go to the later position. The first tier keeps SMITH ahead of an initial or an unlisted token: SMITH has a few thousand given-name uses in the 2020 lists, so its share is just under 1, while an unlisted token’s share is exactly 1.

cd <- get_census_data(c("TAYLOR", "JORDAN"))
determine_surname(cd)   # position of the surname: JORDAN is first, TAYLOR the surname
#> [1] 1

Rules by number of tokens

One token

A lone token is treated as the surname.

show(c("SMITH", "MADONNA"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
SMITH SMITH
MADONNA MADONNA

Two tokens

Most two-word names are written first name first, so the written order is the starting point. The tokens are swapped only when the census makes it much more likely that the name is written surname first.

Each token gets a smoothed surname share,

s=surname count+afirst-name count+surname count+2a,a=20,s = \frac{\text{surname count} + a}{\text{first-name count} + \text{surname count} + 2a}, \quad a = 20,

so a token with few records moves toward 0.5 and thin evidence cannot decide the order on its own. A token in neither census list gets s = 0.85 (an unlisted word is more often a rare surname than a rare given name), and a lone letter gets s = 0.05. The odds that the name is written surname first are

s1(1−s2)(1−s1)s2,\frac{s_1 (1 - s_2)}{(1 - s_1)\, s_2},

and the tokens are swapped when these odds exceed 30. An unlisted first token of one or two letters is initials (HM CHERRY, DC ALLEN).

show(c("JOHN SMITH", "SMITH JOHN", "JORDAN TAYLOR", "TAYLOR JORDAN",
       "LESLIE JAMES", "HARRIS MORRISON", "RICHARD RUVIN", "R BLINCOE"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
JOHN SMITH JOHN SMITH
SMITH JOHN JOHN SMITH
JORDAN TAYLOR JORDAN TAYLOR
TAYLOR JORDAN TAYLOR JORDAN
LESLIE JAMES LESLIE JAMES
HARRIS MORRISON HARRIS MORRISON
RICHARD RUVIN RICHARD RUVIN
R BLINCOE R BLINCOE

Before version 0.2.0 the token with the higher surname share was the surname, wherever it stood. That turned HARRIS MORRISON into MORRISON HARRIS and, because RUVIN has a few first-name records and no surname records in the census lists, RICHARD RUVIN into first name RUVIN.

The settings (a, the unlisted share and the odds) were tuned on 758,388 two-word Form 990 Part VII names, each labelled by the convention of the other names on the same return (LAST, FIRST, FIRST M LAST and the like): see data-raw/name_order_eval.R. On those labels the order errors fell from 12,463 to 2,687. Names written first name first keep their order 99.8% of the time, and 89% of names written surname first are swapped. The rest of the surname-first names, such as WALTER DALE, cannot be told apart from the census counts alone.

A title that is also a surname (SHERIFF, BISHOP, BROTHER) as the first of two tokens is treated as a title when the other token is not mostly a given name. BISHOP JOHN is left alone, because it may be JOHN BISHOP written surname first.

show(c("HM CHERRY", "NICKHATH SHERIFF", "HOWARD SITRON", "SHERIFF MASRY",
       "BISHOP JOHN"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
HM CHERRY HM CHERRY
NICKHATH SHERIFF NICKHATH SHERIFF
HOWARD SITRON HOWARD SITRON
SHERIFF MASRY MASRY
BISHOP JOHN JOHN BISHOP

Three tokens with two initials

The full token is the surname and the initials are the first and middle initials, in order: A J SMITH and SMITH A J both give A J SMITH.

Three tokens with one initial

A single-letter token is a middle initial (or a first initial). The rules assume two orders, FIRST M LAST and LAST FIRST M:

  • a trailing initial means the name was written surname first: SMITH JOHN A becomes JOHN A SMITH;
  • an initial in the middle is reordered only when the two full words pass the two-word written-order test above (SMITH J ALAN becomes J ALAN SMITH);
  • otherwise the order is kept.
show(c("JOHN A SMITH", "SMITH JOHN A", "SMITH J ALAN", "J ALAN SMITH"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
JOHN A SMITH JOHN A SMITH
SMITH JOHN A JOHN A SMITH
SMITH J ALAN J ALAN SMITH
J ALAN SMITH J ALAN SMITH

The trailing-initial rule cannot tell JOHN SMITH A (given name first, stray initial at the end) from SMITH JOHN A, and reads both as surname first.

Three full tokens

The first and last words get the two-word written-order test above. The name is read surname first (SMITH JOHN ALAN becomes JOHN ALAN SMITH) only when the first word is much more likely a surname and the last a given name; otherwise the written order is kept: first, middle, last. DONG JOON YI and TOKS MALIK ASHIRU keep their order.

Up to version 0.2.1 the rule reordered any name whose first word read as a surname and whose second did not, and counted every word missing from the census as a surname. Labelled by the convention of the other names on the same return, 28,811 three-word Part VII names were reordered wrongly 1,210 times by that rule and 53 times by the written-order test (data-raw/name_order_eval3.R).

show(c("JOHN ALAN SMITH", "SMITH JOHN ALAN", "DONG JOON YI", "TOKS MALIK ASHIRU"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
JOHN ALAN SMITH JOHN ALAN SMITH
SMITH JOHN ALAN JOHN ALAN SMITH
DONG JOON YI DONG JOON YI
TOKS MALIK ASHIRU TOKS MALIK ASHIRU

Four or more tokens

The first token is the first name and determine_surname() picks the surname; a single letter is chosen only when nothing else can be. Everything else is the middle name. A word, two or more initials and a word (GLYNN C W SCOTT) is treated as a two-word name with middle initials. If the name opens with two surnames followed by a given name (SMITH JONES MARY ANN), the two surnames are joined into one.

show(c("JOHN PAUL GEORGE RINGO", "SMITH JONES MARY ANN"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
JOHN PAUL GEORGE RINGO JOHN PAUL GEORGE RINGO
SMITH JONES MARY ANN MARY ANN SMITH-JONES

Compound surnames

Compound surnames are kept together by joining their parts with a dash, so they stay one token through the rest of the parse. The census looks names up with the dashes removed (VON-KAMECKE as VONKAMECKE).

Surname particles

prep_name() and fix_locative_surnames() join a particle to the word after it. The particles are LA, VON, VAN, VANDER, DEL, DE, DI, DEN, DER and O, plus ST inside a name (Saint) and LO GRANDE. A second set joins only after the first word and before a word that is not a title: VANDEN, VANDE, SAN, SANTA, LOS, LAS, DELLA, DALLA, DELA, DOS, DAS, DA, DU, TEN and TER (PATRICIA SAN PEDRO, ESTELLA DE LOS RIOS, LEANA DA SILVA). Some of these are also given names, so they are not joined at the start of a name.

A split MC surname inside a name is joined without a dash, the way the census and most records spell it: STEVE MC CORMICK gives MCCORMICK. A leading MC is read as initials (MC OLSON), and a trailing one as a credential (Navy Medical Corps).

Particles chain, so DE LA ROSA and VAN DER BERG become one token.

fix_locative_surnames(c("Jane Van Dyke", "Carlos De La Rosa", "Dylan Van"))
#> [1] "Jane Van-Dyke"     "Carlos De-La-Rosa" "Dylan Van"
show(c("THOMAS H VON KAMECKE", "SEAN ST CLAIR", "JULIA DI BUSSOLO",
       "JUAN CARLOS DE LA ROSA", "MARY VAN DER BERG", "PATRICIA SAN PEDRO",
       "ESTELLA DE LOS RIOS"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
THOMAS H VON KAMECKE THOMAS H VON-KAMECKE
SEAN ST CLAIR SEAN ST-CLAIR
JULIA DI BUSSOLO JULIA DI-BUSSOLO
JUAN CARLOS DE LA ROSA JUAN CARLOS DE-LA-ROSA
MARY VAN DER BERG MARY VAN-DER-BERG
PATRICIA SAN PEDRO PATRICIA SAN-PEDRO
ESTELLA DE LOS RIOS ESTELLA DE-LOS-RIOS

A particle at the end of a name (Dylan Van) has nothing to join and is left alone. ST at the start of a name is not joined, because there it is usually a title.

Two surnames: middle tokens that read as surnames

After the first, middle and last names are assigned, a middle name of three or more letters is checked again. A middle word joins the last name only when at least 90% of its census records are surnames, or it is not in the census. An initial never joins. So MARIA GARCIA LOPEZ gives GARCIA-LOPEZ (GARCIA is 99.8% surname), but JOHN LEE SMITH keeps LEE as the middle name (LEE is 81% surname; up to 0.2.1 this gave LEE-SMITH):

  • one middle token that is a strong surname joins the last name;
  • with several middle tokens, an initial followed by a full token keeps the initial as the middle name and joins the rest to the surname;
  • otherwise, everything from the first surname-like middle token on joins the surname, and the tokens before it stay as the middle name.

When the surname parts are next to each other in the original string, they are joined in the order they were written. MARY ANN SMITH JONES gives SMITH-JONES, even though SMITH was picked as the main surname. When they are not next to each other, the middle part goes first.

show(c("MARIA GARCIA LOPEZ", "JOHN LEE SMITH", "ELIZABETH ANNE WALKER SMITH",
       "JOHN Q PUBLIC SMITH", "MARY ANN SMITH JONES", "JEAN A DU PONT"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
MARIA GARCIA LOPEZ MARIA GARCIA-LOPEZ
JOHN LEE SMITH JOHN LEE SMITH
ELIZABETH ANNE WALKER SMITH ELIZABETH ANNE WALKER-SMITH
JOHN Q PUBLIC SMITH JOHN Q PUBLIC-SMITH
MARY ANN SMITH JONES MARY ANN SMITH-JONES
JEAN A DU PONT JEAN A DU-PONT

One exception: MAY is a common middle name and a surname. If it ends up at the front of a compound surname, it is moved back to the middle name.

show(c("SARAH MAY WILSON", "MARY MAY"))
name first_name middle_name last_name
SARAH MAY WILSON SARAH MAY WILSON
MARY MAY MARY MAY

Titles that turned out to be names

When a token is both a title and a name (EARL, MAJOR), cleaning may strip it and leave no first name. The parser then puts it back, using its position in the original string: a leading token is the first name and a trailing one is the surname. See vignette("name-cleaning").

Limits

  • The rules know only how common each token is, not which order a source uses. If you know the source writes LAST FIRST, reorder the tokens before parsing.
  • Tokens absent from the census rank above names that are mostly given names, so an unlisted given name (SEOKJIN) next to a common given name can end up as the surname (SEOKJIN JAMES -> surname SEOKJIN). In names of three or more words, strong surnames rank above unlisted tokens (TSHEPO CHO keeps CHO), but a name with a large given-name share does not: in LUDWIG VAN BEETHOVEN the unlisted VAN-BEETHOVEN is the surname, as it should be, because LUDWIG is also a given name.
  • A name that is both a common given name and a common surname (JAMES, LESLIE, TAYLOR, JORDAN) is decided by a small margin. Treat such parses as uncertain.
  • A middle word that is mostly a surname (ANNE WALKER, 96%) is joined to the last name. That is right for Spanish and Portuguese double surnames and for maiden names kept as a middle name, but not for a given middle name that is a strong surname. Middle names that are often given names (LEE, RAY, GRANT) stay middle names, so a real double surname made of them is split.
  • A given name missing from the census before a listed name can still be read as a surname written first (CHIYA AYDIN AYHAN, MASSUMEH FARHAD).
